newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shares rise as home-front tension ebbs.
newsitem.headline: German shares rise as home-front tension ebbs.

text.p: German shares posted minor gains on Thursday amid relief that the Bundesbank and Bonn seemed close to reconciliation in their spat over asset revaluation, easing fears of a soft start for monetary union.
The 30-share DAX ended the bourse session up 11.19 points at 3,673.03 points, buoyed by selective interest in individual shares -- most notably airline Deutsche Lufthansa.

Traders said the market jitters that hurt German shares earlier this week eased after the government seemed to bow to the Bundesbank by agreeing to delay receiving returns from revalued assets until 1998, too late for the process to impact Germany's qualification for monetary union.
"The important thing is that they seem to have found an amicable solution," said Josh Waiblinger, assistant vice president of equities at BHF-Bank.
"The Bundesbank appears to have won this one," said another dealer.
The gains were underpinned by a relatively strong performance by Bunds, after leaks of a German unemplyment report due on Friday indicated that joblessness in May was weaker than expected.
Trading was thin as the lack of convincing news and prospect of key jobs data from the U.S. as well as Germany tomorrow kept many investors on hold, dealers said.

There was little reaction to first-quarter GDP data, which showed growth of 0.5 percent from the previous quarter and 1.4 percent year on year, slightly ahead of some expectations but not enough to pressure the market, dealers said.
Lufthansa rose sharply to end up 1.30 marks or more than four percent at 30.80 marks.
Dealers said there was no single reason for its gains, but said sentiment regarding the share was generally good.
One trader said this could mark a phase of interest in Lufthansa, as investors might be trying to push the airline's price higher before the government sells as stake in it later this year.
"Lufthansa strikes me as a clear buy," he said.
Steelmaker Thyssen AG rose 2.60 marks to 411 marks, despite a downgrade by Salomon Brothers. Other analysts had been raising their estimates on the stock, dealers said.
